value.body: A Company Secretary keeps a company on the right side of company and securities law. Listed and larger companies hire one in-house, and others work as practising CSs serving several clients. A typical day involves preparing board and shareholder meeting papers, writing minutes, and making filings with the Registrar of Companies and stock exchanges.

items.label: Qualification
items.note: CSEET → Executive → Professional, plus practical training

items.label: Who must appoint one
items.value: Listed companies and companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more

items.label: Common tools
items.value: MCA21 portal, stock exchange filing portals, Excel

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Join ICSI's CS course: clear CSEET (some graduates and CA/CMA qualifiers are exempt), then the Executive and Professional levels, and complete the required practical training. A B.Com or law background helps but any stream can take the course. Freshers usually start as an assistant or junior CS; practising independently needs a Certificate of Practice from ICSI.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Reading and applying the Companies Act and SEBI regulations
Drafting board resolutions, notices and minutes
Making ROC and stock exchange filings on time
Keeping statutory registers and compliance calendars

value.title: At a glance
items: Common next roles are senior CS, compliance head, or company secretary of a listed company.
Practising CSs do secretarial audits, incorporations and compliance work for many clients.
The course takes several years for most students, and pass rates at the higher levels are low.
Work peaks around board meetings, AGMs and filing deadlines.

competition.note: B.Com graduates in 2023-24 at institutions that reported to AISHE — everyone finishing that degree, not only those entering this role.
